studies.title: Not Worth Mentioning Yet
studies.meaning: The surah opens with a question that is really a reminder of an absence. There was a stretch of time in which you were not a thing anybody spoke of. Then four short statements build a person: made from a mingled drop, made to be tested, given hearing and sight, shown the road. The two senses are named in the same breath as the testing, which ties the equipment to the purpose. And the fork in the third ayah is stated with complete evenness, grateful or ungrateful, without weighting either side.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though several classical authorities call it Meccan and the reports differ. The opening question addresses the human being in general rather than any audience in particular, which is why the classification has never been easy to settle. What the surah goes on to describe, a household giving away its food, belongs to a settled community rather than to a persecuted one.

keyTerms.note: A word for extended time, distinct from the ordinary word for a period. Pre-Islamic Arabs used it for the impersonal passage of time that wears everything down, which makes its appearance in this opening pointed.
The second word is a plural adjective for things blended together. It occurs once in the Quran, and it describes the starting material as already a mixture rather than a single simple substance.
A definite noun for a path already laid. Guidance is described as showing somebody a road that exists rather than as making him walk it, which is what leaves the following fork genuinely open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs kept genealogies as their main form of memory, and a man existed publicly by being named in one. To be unmentioned was to be nobody, and the phrase in the opening ayah uses exactly that measure. The audience did not need the concept explained. They would have understood immediately that the surah begins by placing every listener, however well connected, on the far side of the first line of his own family tree.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a mingled drop in the second ayah occurs once in the whole Quran. It is a plural adjective attached to a singular noun, which Arabic grammarians discuss, and the effect is to describe the smallest visible beginning of a person as already plural: not one thing, but several things blended before anything was formed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The opening establishes the human being as a recent arrival before establishing anything else about him. That ordering matters: everything the surah later says about reward, effort and reluctance rests on a creature who was, quite recently, not being spoken of at all. The senses are given as test equipment rather than as gifts, and the two possible responses are named in the same sentence, so the passage builds a person and leaves him undecided.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same reminder as a question: did the human being forget he was nothing before.
Lists the same equipment, eyes and a tongue, and then names the two roads shown.
Traces the same sequence from a fluid beginning to hearing, sight and hearts being given.

studies.applyIt: Find the oldest photograph in your house of somebody nobody living remembers. Look at it for a minute. That person was mentioned constantly once, and now is not. The surah opens by putting you on the other side of that line and asks you to start from there rather than from the middle of your own life.

studies.title: A Meal For Three Strangers
studies.meaning: The reward is described before the reason, and then the reason turns out to be small and specific. A drink, a spring the drinkers themselves open. Then three lines of description: they keep vows, they fear a day whose harm spreads wide, and they give food away. Scholars differ over the phrase attached to the food, reading it as giving despite loving the food itself, or as giving out of love for God, and both readings are old.
studies.historicalContext: The tradition this collection follows calls the surah Medinan, though several classical authorities call it Meccan. Reports tie these ayat to a household that gave away its food on three nights running. The sources differ over who was involved. What the wording itself shows is the setting. Captives in that society were fed by the households that held them.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning wide open land, and behind the words for goodness and for dutifulness to parents. It names generosity of character rather than correctness, which suits a passage about giving food.

An intensive verb for splitting ground so water bursts out. The drinkers are given the action, so the spring is described as opened by them rather than found, which is unusual in a description of paradise.
From the root for a bird taking off. It describes harm that scatters in every direction rather than harm that is large, which is a different kind of fear.
A prisoner taken in conflict, from a root meaning to bind. Listing him third, after the poor and the orphan, extends the feeding to someone who was recently an enemy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Captives in seventh-century Arabia were housed with families rather than in prisons. The household fed them from its own pot. That put an enemy at the same meal in a year when food might be short. The three people named in this ayah are a poor man, an orphan and a captive. They are the three with no claim on anyone: no earnings, no father, no tribe present to speak for them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for what the cup is mixed with occurs only once in the Quran, here. It names a cool, scented substance used in the region for perfume and for preserving. Two ayat later the same passage names the reason for the reward, and it is a bowl of food handed to three people. The distance between the two descriptions is deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a huge reward beside a very small act, and does not apologise for the gap. That is the point being made about how God deals with people. It also picks its recipients with care. The three named have nothing to give back and no power to repay, so the act cannot be an investment in a relationship. And the vow kept in the line before makes it a portrait of promises honoured when nobody could enforce them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the words of the people described here, refusing both payment and gratitude in advance.
Names the same act as the steep road, and specifies the day on which it costs something.
Uses the same construction about giving what you love, in a longer list of what righteousness is.

studies.applyIt: Give away food this week rather than money, and give it to someone who cannot thank you usefully. Cook something extra, or hand a meal to a person you will not see again. The ayah names food, and food has a quality money does not. You had to want it yourself for the giving to register.
studies.explainEasier: Good people will drink from a cup at a spring in the garden. They kept their promises. They were afraid of a hard day. They gave their food to poor people, to orphans, and to prisoners.

studies.title: No Payment, No Thanks
studies.meaning: Their words are quoted, and the striking thing is what they refuse. Not payment only, but thanks, which is the currency generosity usually runs on. Then the account of what follows uses three verbs of God's doing: He guarded them, He met them with brightness and gladness, and He repaid them. What He repays is named as their patience rather than their giving, so the endurance behind the act is what is credited.
studies.historicalContext: The tradition this collection follows calls the surah Medinan, though the classical authorities differ. Reports attach the passage to a household that gave away its food, and they vary in detail. What the sentence itself keeps is a piece of speech. These are the words a giver says to a recipient. The Quran rarely records that from an ordinary person rather than from a prophet.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for doing something for God alone, using the word for a face. The tradition takes it as naming the direction of an act rather than a part of God, and the whole phrase means for His sake.

Refusing this is the sharper half of the sentence. Payment can be declined without cost, but declining a recipient's gratitude removes the last thing a giver usually keeps, which is being known to have given.
A rare five-letter word describing a face contracted with strain, paired here with a word for scowling. Arabic builds longer words for heavier meanings, and this is among the longest in the Quran.
The word for the bloom on a plant with enough water, used of a face that looks well. It answers the drawn, contracted face of the day they feared, feature for feature.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving in Arabia was rarely private. A generous man was named in poetry, and the naming was part of the deal. Hospitality bought standing as much as it fed anyone. Refusing thanks in that culture was not modesty. It was opting out of the whole system by which giving was repaid. The sentence quoted here would have sounded strange to the person taking the food.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran almost always quotes prophets, angels, or opponents. Here it quotes two sentences from unnamed believers speaking to a poor man at their door, and preserves them exactly. It is one of a very small number of places where ordinary people's words are recorded as scripture, and what they say is a refusal rather than a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined here by subtraction. The passage does not describe an inner state; it lists what the givers declined to take, and the list ends with the one thing almost nobody declines. That makes sincerity checkable in principle: it shows up in what you refuse rather than in what you feel. The reward is then attached to patience, which quietly says that the refusing was the difficult part.

crossReferences.why: Names the failure this speech avoids, a gift undone afterwards by being mentioned to the person who received it.
Describes the same motive in the same words, adding that no one has any claim on him being repaid.
Gives the act these words accompany, food handed to a poor man, an orphan and a captive.

studies.applyIt: Do one good thing this week and take active steps to keep it unknown. Not just refrain from mentioning it; arrange it so nobody can trace it back to you. Then notice the small pull to leave a clue. That pull is what the sentence in this ayah is declining, and it is easier to see once you have felt it.
studies.explainEasier: The people who gave their food said they did it only for God. They wanted no payment and no thanks. They were afraid of a hard day. So God kept them safe from it, and gave them a garden.

studies.title: Neither Sun Nor Bitter Cold
studies.meaning: The description works by removing the two extremes a body actually suffers. No sun, no piercing cold, and the word for the second occurs once in the Quran. Then everything is brought within reach: shade lowered over them, fruit made docile enough to take without standing. The vessels are described with a small paradox, crystal made of silver, and the last clause says the servers measured them exactly. Commentators note that even the portions are fitted to the drinker rather than poured generously.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though the classical authorities differ. The passage belongs to the surah's long description of what the righteous receive, which follows directly on the account of a household giving its food away. The imagery answers, item by item, the discomforts of that climate, which is a consistent feature of how the earliest descriptions of the garden are built.

keyTerms.note: A word for intense cold, occurring once in the Quran. Arabic lexicographers connect it to the coldest part of the year, and pairing it with the sun covers the whole range of what weather does to a body.
The verb and its cognate noun both come from the root for being made docile, used of an animal broken to the hand. Fruit is described as tamed, so reaching is unnecessary rather than merely easy.
The name of a root traded into Arabia from the east and valued as a warming spice. It occurs once in the Quran, and it sits in a description that has just ruled out cold entirely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both extremes named here were real. Desert days burned and desert nights could freeze, and the same journey might require shade by noon and every blanket by dawn. Shade was property: a tree by a well was worth fighting over, and the right to sit under it was negotiated. Silver vessels were the furniture of kings, and glass was an import most people had only heard described.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the words in this short passage occur once each in the whole Quran: the word for biting cold, the word for ginger, and the name of the spring in the ayah just after. The description of the garden here is built partly out of vocabulary that the Book uses exactly once and never again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes reward largely by subtraction and by proximity. What is promised is not abundance piled up but the removal of exertion: nothing too hot, nothing too cold, nothing out of reach, nothing mismeasured. That is a specific claim about what the trouble with this life actually is. It locates it not in scarcity but in effort, distance and the constant work of adjusting to conditions that do not fit.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of clusters hanging low enough to be taken without effort.
Uses the same word for glass, in the palace floor that a visiting queen mistook for water.
Describes the same furnishings and vessels, with drink that causes neither headache nor exhaustion.

studies.applyIt: Pay attention to one physical discomfort today that you normally push through without naming: the room too cold, the chair wrong, the light in your eyes. Fix it, if you can, in ten seconds. This passage describes relief in exactly those terms, and most of us have stopped noticing how much of the day we spend enduring small things.

studies.title: Wherever You Look
studies.meaning: A spring is named rather than described, and the name occurs once in the Quran and nowhere else in Arabic before it, which is why the lexicographers wrote so much about it. Then the attendants, compared to pearls scattered rather than strung, so the image is of movement and dispersal rather than arrangement. The last ayah changes the grammar and addresses the reader directly: wherever you look. It is the only ayah in the description that puts the reader inside it and asks him to turn his head.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though several classical authorities call the surah Meccan. These three ayat come near the end of the surah's account of the reward, immediately before the description of what the righteous are wearing. No specific occasion is reported for them. The description is general and belongs to the surah's larger answer to the household that gave away its food.

keyTerms.note: A name given to a spring, occurring once in the Quran. The early lexicographers connect its sound to water that goes down easily and to a smooth flow, and they treat it as a name rather than a description.
A passive participle from the verb to make something endure. Commentators divide over whether it means kept from ageing or kept permanently in that service, and both readings are preserved.
A participle for something strewn loose rather than gathered. Pearls are normally described strung; describing them scattered turns an image of value into an image of motion across a room.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water in Arabia was named. Wells and springs carried proper names, were owned by clans, and appear in poetry the way landmarks do, since knowing which water lay along which road was the difference between arriving and not. Naming a spring rather than describing it was therefore the most natural way to make it real, and an audience would have heard a place they could ask directions to.
studies.didYouKnow: The name of the spring in the first of these ayat occurs once in the Quran, and the early Arabic lexicographers had no earlier attested use to work from, so they reasoned from its sound alone. Several of them describe it as a word whose syllables imitate water running easily, which is an unusual kind of argument to find in a dictionary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The turn to the second person in the last ayah does something the rest of the description cannot. It stops listing and puts the reader in the middle of a room with instructions to look around. What he is told he will find is not itemised, only that it is everywhere and that it is a kingdom. That leaves the promise open at exactly the point where more detail would have closed it down.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same comparison for the attendants, describing them as well-guarded pearls.
Names another drink by its source, a spring from which those brought near will drink.
Promises whatever they wish there, and more besides, without itemising what the more is.

studies.applyIt: Try the instruction literally once today. Stop where you are, and look around the room slowly, at everything rather than at what you came in for. The ayah's promise is about what a person sees when he is not looking for anything. Most of us never do that in a place we already know.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: And Their Lord Gave Them Drink
studies.meaning: The ayah lists three things and then does something the rest of the description has not done. Green silk, heavy brocade, silver bracelets: all of it is passive, given to them by unnamed hands. Then the final clause changes the subject of the sentence. Their Lord gave them to drink. Commentators dwell on this, noting that every other cup in the surah is carried round by servants, and only this one is attributed to God directly, which is what makes the drink pure in a sense the word carries elsewhere of cleansing.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though the classical authorities differ over the surah. This single ayah closes the description of the reward before the surah turns to address the Prophet. It answers, point for point, the ayat earlier in the surah describing a household that gave its own food away and refused both payment and thanks for it.

keyTerms.note: A word for thin silk, borrowed into Arabic from further east. It names an import that reached Arabia through the trade routes and would have been known chiefly by reputation rather than by touch.
Thick silk shot with gold thread, again a loanword. Pairing it with the lighter silk covers both ends of a fabric range the audience knew as the clothing of foreign courts.

An intensive form that means both clean in itself and cleansing of whatever it touches. The Quran uses it elsewhere of rain sent down from the sky, and in both places the sense is water that purifies rather than water that is merely clean.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Silk in Arabia was foreign and famous. It arrived along the routes from Persia and beyond, and most people in Mecca or Medina had heard it described more often than they had seen it, as the dress of kings in places they would never go. Silver bracelets were more familiar, worn as portable wealth. The ayah dresses ordinary people in what the audience thought of as court clothing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the drink in this ayah occurs twice in the Quran. The other place describes rain sent down from the sky as pure water, which is the ordinary miracle available to everyone. The same adjective is used for what a person is given directly by his Lord in the garden and for the water that falls on a field.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The shift in the last clause is the whole point of the ayah. Everything else is delivered by attendants, and one thing is not, which makes the reward relational rather than material at its highest point. The description of the drink as purifying also implies that something is still being removed even there. And the ayah quietly answers the earlier passage: people who refused thanks from those they fed are served by God Himself.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for purity, of rain sent down from the sky as mercy.
States what these people refused: no payment and no thanks from anyone they fed.
Describes the same green silk and brocade, with bracelets, as the dress of the garden.

studies.applyIt: Notice who actually hands you things. Most of what reaches you today will come through somebody else, and you will thank the hands rather than the source. Pick one ordinary thing that arrives today, a meal, a glass of water, and take it slowly enough to think past the person who passed it to you.

studies.title: Your Effort Is Appreciated
studies.meaning: A sentence is spoken to them and the second half is unexpected: their striving is described as having been thanked. The word is the one used of a person acknowledging a favour, and it is applied here to God receiving human effort. Then the surah turns abruptly to the Prophet with three instructions in a row. Wait for your Lord's judgement; do not yield to a sinner or an ingrate among them; keep the Name in your mouth at both ends of the day. The reward has just been described, and the instruction is to wait for it.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though several classical authorities call the surah Meccan. The instruction not to yield suggests pressure from identifiable individuals rather than general hostility, and the sources describe such approaches at various points in the mission. No single occasion is attached to these ayat with agreement, and the commentators generally read them as a turn from description to address.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from the verb to give thanks, applied to human effort with God as the one giving them. The reversal is deliberate: the word usually runs the other way, from creature to Creator.
A verbal noun reinforcing the verb before it, and the verb form used implies portions rather than a single act. The grammar carries the fact that the revelation arrived over years.
Two words naming the early part of the day and the stretch between afternoon and sunset. Arabic uses the pair to mean the whole day by naming its two ends, not two scheduled moments.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pressure in that society came through relationships rather than through force. A man was approached by someone whose family had a claim on his, or who had done his father a favour, and the request arrived wrapped in obligation that was very hard to refuse without insult. The instruction here names two kinds of person to hold out against, and both would have come with exactly that kind of standing behind them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing human striving as thanked appears in the Quran only as a passive participle in this construction, and always with God as the one doing the thanking. The Book that repeatedly asks people to be grateful uses the same root, a handful of times, for God's response to what they do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange described in the first ayah runs in an unfamiliar direction. Effort is not merely accepted or rewarded; it is thanked, which implies something received rather than something owed. Then the instructions that follow ask for patience precisely after the reward has been described in detail, which is the harder order. Knowing what is coming does not shorten the wait, and the remedy prescribed is not reflection but a name kept on the tongue.

crossReferences.why: Names God as appreciative and knowing, using the same root for His response to people.
States that the recitation was divided into portions to be delivered slowly, over time.
Instructs him to stay with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, and not to look past them.

studies.applyIt: Say the Name once at the start of your day and once when the light begins to go. Not a long session, two moments. The instruction here marks the two ends of the day rather than a time set aside, and the point is to bracket everything in between rather than to withdraw from it.

studies.title: They Leave A Heavy Day Behind
studies.meaning: The instruction continues into the night with two verbs, prostrating and declaring God beyond fault, and the second is given a long stretch rather than a fixed portion. Then the contrast arrives, and it is phrased spatially rather than morally. These people love what is immediate and leave a heavy Day behind their backs. The last ayah answers that with a statement about the body: We made them and We knotted their frame tight, and We could exchange them for others like them whenever We chose.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though the classical authorities differ. These ayat close the surah's address to the Prophet and turn back to the people around him. The description of leaving the Day behind names an attitude rather than a group, which is why the commentators apply it broadly rather than tying it to particular individuals or to a reported occasion.

keyTerms.note: A feminine adjective for what comes quickly, used as a name for the present world. It names this life by its speed rather than by its substance, which is the whole of the criticism.
A word for what is behind a person and out of sight. Placing the Day there makes the failure a matter of orientation: it is not denied, it is simply positioned where nobody has to look.
From a root for binding and for a captive held fast. It names the body as a structure knotted together, and the word occurs once in the Quran in this sense.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night was the only part of the day that belonged to a person. Work ran from light to light, and the hours after the last meal were when a household finally had itself to itself. Choosing to spend a long stretch of that standing was a real cost, not a spiritual gesture, and everyone in that society would have measured it in the tiredness of the following morning's work.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the body's frame in the last of these ayat comes from the root that gives Arabic its word for a captive taken in war, because a captive is somebody bound. The ayah describes a human being as tightly tied together, and the same root names the condition of a man in ropes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three ayat move from devotion, to a diagnosis, to a statement about replacement, and the sequence is not accidental. What is criticised is not disbelief but preference, a choice about which of two things to keep in view. The closing line then removes any sense that the arrangement is owed to anyone. The same power that knotted a body together could exchange it, which makes the night standing a response rather than a transaction.

crossReferences.why: States the same preference in nearly identical words: you love the fleeting and leave the Hereafter.
Says God could remove people and bring others, and is able to do exactly that.
Assigns part of the night to standing, and describes it as something additional.

studies.applyIt: Give the last ten minutes before sleep to something other than a screen this week. Not an hour, ten minutes. The passage asks for part of the night, and the reason it specifies night is that it is the only stretch nobody else has a claim on. Notice how hard even ten minutes turns out to be.

studies.title: You Cannot Will Unless He Wills
studies.meaning: Three ayat that appear to pull in opposite directions and are left standing together. The first hands the choice to the reader: whoever wills takes a road. The second says nobody wills except within God's willing. The third describes God admitting whom He wills into His mercy and preparing punishment for the wrongdoers. Commentators have written extensively here and the mainstream position is to affirm both statements without collapsing one into the other, noting that the names closing the second ayah are knowledge and wisdom rather than power.
studies.historicalContext: Classified as Medinan in the tradition this collection follows, though the classical authorities differ over the surah as a whole. These are its closing ayat, arriving after a full description of reward, a set of instructions to the Prophet, and a diagnosis of those around him. The same pairing of human willing and divine willing closes several other short surahs, which suggests a settled way of ending rather than an occasion.

keyTerms.note: The noun for something that brings back what was already known. Using it here makes the surah's whole description of reward and loss a recollection rather than information newly supplied.
The first of the two names closing the ayah about willing. Choosing knowledge rather than power at this point shifts the emphasis from what God can impose to what He knows about the one willing.
The second name, from a root that also gives the word for a bridle. It names not merely knowing what is right but putting things where they belong, which is what the pairing with knowledge is doing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic had a settled vocabulary for fate, and pre-Islamic poetry is full of time as an impersonal force that strikes without reason and cannot be appealed to. That is the background these ayat are written against. What they put in its place is not an impersonal law but a will attached to knowledge and wisdom, which is a different thing to live under, and the audience would have felt the substitution.
studies.didYouKnow: The first of these ayat appears word for word in another early surah, where it closes a long passage of warning just before that chapter's final ayah. The Quran reuses the sentence intact rather than rephrasing it, and both times it arrives at the moment the pressure is released and the matter handed to the hearer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two statements are left unreconciled on purpose, and the choice of divine names is the clue to how they are meant to be held. Knowledge and wisdom, rather than might, close the ayah about willing, which frames the relation as one of understanding rather than of override. Practically, the passage gives a reader both things he needs: a road he can take today, and the knowledge that taking it was never entirely his own doing.

crossReferences.why: Closes another early surah with the identical sentence about whoever wills taking a path.
Pairs human willing with God's willing in the same construction at a surah's end.
States the fork plainly: let whoever wishes believe and whoever wishes refuse.

studies.applyIt: Take the first sentence at face value today and do one small thing you have been leaving to a better version of yourself. Then, when it is done, resist giving yourself the credit. The passage puts those two moves side by side and does not explain how they fit, which is roughly how they feel from the inside.
